questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Introducing yourself and the register it calls for
questions.learningObjective: choose the introduction that fits a first meeting at work
questions.stem: At a first meeting a new colleague says: « Bonjour, je m'appelle Amina Diallo, je viens de Dakar. » Which pair of features marks the register as a first professional meeting?

options.text: « Bonjour » and the full « je m'appelle », both the expected choices with a stranger at work
« Bonjour » and « je viens de », which would sound out of place in any first introduction
options.misconception: reads a place of origin as a marker of an informal tone when it is ordinary content

options.text: « je m'appelle » and « je viens de », which are forms reserved for family conversations
options.misconception: believes two everyday constructions can only be used with relatives

options.text: « Amina Diallo » and « Dakar », which show the speaker is talking to a child
options.misconception: reads a full name and a town as markers of familiarity rather than of formality

questions.explanation: A French speaker does not move to « tu » and to the first name until the older or more senior person offers it, so a first meeting at work is done in the vous, with the surname and with a set phrase such as « je m'appelle ». « Je viens de Dakar » adds no register at all, since giving a place of origin is ordinary in any introduction whatever. The trap is reading a detail of content as a detail of tone: neither the surname nor the town says anything about how familiar the two people are meant to be.
questions.hint: Ask which word in the sentence is a choice rather than a fact about the speaker.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Greetings and the hours they belong to
questions.learningObjective: match a greeting to the hour at which it is used
questions.stem: A visitor reaches a French office at half past seven in the evening and the receptionist says: « Bonsoir, je vous écoute. » Which greeting belongs to that hour, and on what grounds?

options.text: « Bonsoir », the greeting that takes over from the late afternoon through the night
« Bonjour », the only greeting French uses before the middle of the day
options.misconception: fixes the morning greeting as the sole daytime greeting and ignores the evening one

options.text: « Salut », a greeting reserved for people who work a night shift together
options.misconception: calls an informal greeting a marker of a night shift rather than of familiarity

options.text: « Bonsoir », a formula whose only job in French is to say goodbye in the evening
options.misconception: confuses the evening greeting on arrival with the same word used as a farewell

questions.explanation: French greetings follow the clock, and the change happens in the late afternoon: « bonjour » runs from the morning until the end of the afternoon, and « bonsoir » takes over from then until the night has passed. « Bonsoir » does a second job as an evening farewell, which is why a learner meets it in two places, but « je vous écoute » shows it used on arrival. « Salut » marks a relationship rather than an hour, and the formal « je vous écoute » marks the opposite relationship.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Farewells and the formality they carry
questions.learningObjective: sort farewells by the relationship they assume
questions.stem: Two colleagues part at the end of a long project. Which farewell is the ordinary neutral way to close the day and see the other person again soon?

options.text: « Au revoir, à jeudi », which works at any level and names the next meeting
« Adieu », which is what colleagues say each evening when they separate
options.misconception: reads a literary and almost final farewell as the everyday parting word

options.text: « Salut, à plus », which is the most formal of the three because it is so short
options.misconception: takes a deliberately familiar farewell for a formal one on account of its brevity

options.text: « Ciao », which is the correct French farewell when a colleague leaves for good
options.misconception: assumes an Italian loanword is the standard French workplace farewell

questions.explanation: « Au revoir » is the neutral farewell and can be used with anyone, and adding « à jeudi » turns it into a small promise to meet again. « Adieu » belongs to literature, to speeches and to the idea of parting for good, and a French speaker rarely says it at the door of an office. « Salut, à plus » sits at the informal end and needs the shared familiarity of « salut ». The trap is judging a farewell by its length rather than by the distance it assumes between the two speakers.
questions.hint: Ask which of them could be said to a stranger you will meet again.

questions.learningObjective: select the standard polite question for a name
questions.stem: At a school reception desk a student must ask a stranger their name. Which question is the standard polite way to do it?

« Comment tu t'appelles ? », the form used in a first interview with a stranger
options.misconception: assumes tutoiement is the default and that the informal pronoun is always acceptable

options.text: « Vous êtes quel nom ? », a question standard French uses with any interlocutor
options.misconception: translates a structure from another language and expects French to accept it

options.misconception: asks for the name of a thing rather than the name of the person asked

questions.topic: Ordering a dish in a restaurant

questions.stem: A shopper wants to know what half a kilo of roast will cost at the butcher's counter. Which question asks for that?

« Combien fait le rôti ? », which is a natural question but leaves the amount unstated

options.misconception: puts the weight where the noun belongs, after the amount rather than before it

questions.topic: Agreement of an adjective naming a dish
questions.learningObjective: match an adjective to the gender and number of the noun it describes
questions.stem: A menu line reads « omelette aux champignons frais, servie avec du pain grillé ». Why does the adjective change shape between « frais » and « grillé »?

options.text: « frais » agrees with the masculine plural « champignons », and « grillé » with the masculine singular « pain »
« frais » agrees with « champignons », and « grillé » is untouched because it comes after « servie »
options.misconception: believes an adjective placed after a past participle loses its own agreement

options.text: « frais » takes no agreement, and « grillé » takes an e because it follows « pain »
options.misconception: mixes two unrelated rules about the e and about the number of the noun

options.text: « frais » takes an e before a noun, and « grillé » takes an e because it names a dish
options.misconception: treats the e of a masculine adjective as a marker of a dish rather than of agreement

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.learningObjective: identify the landmark that fixes the moment of a turn
questions.stem: A stranger asks « Pardon, je cherche la gare. » and the reply is « Vous continuez tout droit, puis vous tournez à gauche en face de la pharmacie. » Which part of the reply fixes where the turn is made?

options.text: « en face de la pharmacie », which gives the pharmacy as the point the turn is measured from
« tout droit », which tells the walker to carry on past the point of turning
options.misconception: reads the first instruction as the decisive one and ignores where it stops

options.text: « à gauche », which names the direction the turn is made in
options.misconception: takes the direction alone as enough and misses that no landmark fixes the moment of turning

options.text: « la gare », which names the place the reply has not yet reached
options.misconception: confuses the destination being asked about with a point on the route

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.learningObjective: use a confirmation that lets the speaker correct a mistake
questions.stem: A colleague has explained the new filing system. Which line checks that the explanation landed while still leaving the colleague room to correct you?

options.text: « Si je comprends bien, chaque dossier va dans le classeur rouge, c'est cela ? »
« C'est compris, c'est compris, c'est compris. », which repeats one word to show agreement
options.misconception: believes repeating a single word is a sign that the explanation was understood

options.text: « Je ne comprends pas du tout, recommencez tout. », which asks for the whole thing again
options.misconception: throws away the part that was clear and starts the explanation from nothing

options.text: « D'accord, ça marche, on verra plus tard. », which closes the subject politely
options.misconception: agrees to a postponement nobody proposed and gives the colleague nothing to correct

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.learningObjective: keep the three requests a French speaker finds acceptable
questions.stem: A visitor has not caught the price. Four requests are on the table, and three of them ask for the information again in a form a French speaker would accept without stiffening. Which are those three?

options.text: « Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ? »
« Pourriez-vous redire plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ? »
« Vous pouvez me répéter plus fort, parce que je suis le français. »

options.text: « Je n'ai pas bien compris : pouvez-vous parler plus lentement ? »

questions.topic: Correcting yourself in the middle of a sentence
questions.learningObjective: choose the lightest repair for a slip of the tongue
questions.stem: A speaker begins « Je viens de Bordeaux, enfin, de — » How does a French speaker finish the repair without stopping the sentence?

« Je me trompe : je viens de Rennes. », which announces a standing habit of being wrong
options.misconception: puts the speaker in the habit of error and so overstates a single slip of the tongue

options.text: « Je veux dire pas de Bordeaux, mais non. », which keeps the negation inside the repair
options.misconception: inserts a negation where the repair is meant to replace the name rather than cancel it

options.text: « J'ai dit faux, donc je ne viens pas. », which confesses that the speaker was mistaken
options.misconception: claims the words were false instead of saying the speaker was the one who erred

questions.learningObjective: name the three moves a polite interruption makes at once
questions.stem: During a meeting the second speaker says: « Excusez-moi, je me permets de vous interrompre, est-ce que vous pouvez préciser ce point ? » What does that one sentence manage?

It asks leave to speak and then waits in silence for the floor to be handed over
options.misconception: reads the request as a silent formality and expects no question to follow it

options.text: It claims that the floor already belongs to the speaker and defends that claim
options.misconception: treats the interruption as a claim of right rather than as a request for it

options.misconception: latches on to the apology and gives it a target it was not aimed at

questions.learningObjective: keep a disagreement on the proposal and off the person
questions.stem: A colleague defends a plan you believe is wrong. Which reply disagrees and leaves the disagreement about the plan?

« C'est faux, et vous ne comprenez rien à ce projet. »
options.misconception: attacks the person instead of the proposal and leaves nothing anybody could answer

options.text: « Je crois que vous avez tort, comme d'habitude. »
options.misconception: adds a habitual gibe that turns an argument about a plan into a matter of standing

questions.learningObjective: give a two-part test for the register of a new relationship

questions.topic: Checking a message before sending it
questions.learningObjective: give four checks that catch the faults that cost a message

answer.exemplar: Four checks, and the order is the order of the damage. First, the register: do the greeting, the opening formula and the closing all sit at the same level, since a formal close after an informal greeting is the most common single fault. Second, the request: is there one, and is it a verb, so the reader can see what is being asked rather than what is being reported. Third, the facts: every date, every reference number and every amount read twice against the document they came from, because one wrong date is enough to make a message unbelievable. Fourth, the politeness that costs nothing: a greeting of the day and a closing formula, which are not decoration. What none of these checks is for is style: rewriting a plain sentence in order to sound elegant is the one change that reliably makes a message harder to read.

questions.explanation: Checking is cheap and rewriting is not, so the checks are worth doing in the order in which they prevent the most damage. The register fault is the most common because it is invisible to the writer, who hears the sentence in their own voice. The missing-verb fault produces a message that is pleasant and unanswered, since a reader cannot act on a report. The fact fault is the cheapest to fix and the most damaging to leave, because everything else in the message is then doubted. What to watch is the urge to improve the style while the facts go unchecked.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: « Madame, je suis désolée de vous informer que je dois annuler mon rendez-vous de demain. Deux dates me conviennent mieux : mardi à 10 h ou jeudi à 16 h. Je reste à votre disposition et vous prie de me confirmer la plus commode. » Stage two: the word doing the work is « désolée », and it cannot move to the end because in a French cancellation the apology is a premise rather than a sign-off. « Je suis désolée de vous informer que je dois annuler » announces the apology and the necessity in one breath, and everything after it is possible because of it. Put at the end, the same message would read as a decision taken and a regret attached, which is a refusal dressed as a courtesy. The two new dates matter for the same reason, since an apology with no alternative leaves the reader with a hole in the diary.

questions.explanation: The position of the apology is a French speaker's clearest test of whether a cancellation is meant politely. An apology at the front licenses what follows; an apology at the end reports it. The alternative dates are part of the apology in practice, because they turn a loss into a rearrangement, and a French reader notices their absence more than their wording. What to watch is the necessity, which is better said with « je dois » than with « je ne peux plus », since the first is a fact and the second invites a discussion the cancelling party does not want.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence in your own message a reader would quote to a colleague.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.learningObjective: write a self-introduction and see what the shorter version assumes
questions.stem: Stage one: write the two sentences you would use to introduce yourself to a group you have just joined. Stage two: cut them to one sentence and say what the cut sentence now assumes.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: « Bonjour, je m'appelle Marc Lemoine, je travaille au service après-vente et j'ai rejoint l'équipe il y a trois semaines. J'espère m'y habituer vite. » Stage two: one sentence — « Je suis Marc Lemoine, du service après-vente, nouveau depuis trois semaines. » What the short version now assumes is that a room can be answered with « bonjour » and that the writer's post and his date both fit in a single breath, which they do in a room of nine people and would not in a room of ninety. It also assumes the second sentence was decoration, and it was: « j'espère m'y habituer vite » says nothing a listener can act on, and the group will say it back to him. Cutting it costs nothing and makes the introduction easier to hear.

questions.explanation: Cutting a self-introduction is a useful exercise because the thing that falls away is always the sentence written to be reassuring rather than to inform. French speakers add « j'espère m'y habituer vite » because it seems gracious, and it is gracious, and it is also the line a busy room loses first. The second assumption the short version makes is about the room, since a single sentence of identification suits a small group and a large hall needs the name, the post and the date said separately. What to watch is the greeting, which survives the cut only if the room is small enough to answer it.
questions.hint: Ask which of your two sentences a listener could repeat to somebody else afterwards.
